records.derivation: Set F(theta)=1-3*sin(theta)+5*cos(3*theta), a continuous function. At theta=k*pi/3 for k=0,...,6, the cosine term is 5*(-1)^k and the remaining term lies in [-2,4]. Thus the signs alternate strictly: positive at even k and negative at odd k. The six successive open subintervals contain at least six distinct roots. For completeness put z=cos(theta)+i*sin(theta), so |z|=1 and z is nonzero. Integer polar powers give sin(theta)=(z-z^(-1))/(2i) and cos(3theta)=(z^3+z^(-3))/2. Multiplying the equation by 2*z^3 yields5*z^6+3*i*z^4+2*z^3-3*i*z^2+5=0. This nonzero degree-six polynomial has at most six distinct complex zeros: repeatedly factor z-a for each distinct zero, using the factor theorem and induction, so more than six distinct factors would exceed the degree. The map theta->z is one-to-one on(0,2*pi], and its endpoint z=1 is not a zero. Hence there are exactly six solutions, D. This upper-bound proof does not use the fundamental theorem of algebra or assert that every polynomial has a root.

records.derivation: For x>0, taking logarithms gives F(x)=ln(x)-C*2^x=0, where C=ln(sqrt(2))/2^(sqrt(2))>0. There are no roots at x<=1. One root is a=sqrt(2). Also F(2)=ln(2)*(1-2/2^(sqrt(2)))>0 because sqrt(2)>1, and F(4)=ln(2)*(2-8/2^(sqrt(2)))<0 because sqrt(2)<2. Continuity gives another root beta in (2,4). To prove that these are all roots without unrepresented logarithmic/exponential derivative rules, take distinct u,v>0. AM-GM gives (u+v)/2>sqrt(u*v), hence ln((u+v)/2)>(ln(u)+ln(v))/2; applying AM-GM to 2^u,2^v gives 2^((u+v)/2)<(2^u+2^v)/2. Consequently F((u+v)/2)>(F(u)+F(v))/2. Repeated bisection proves the non-strict chord inequality at every dyadic weight by induction; continuity extends it to every real weight in [0,1]. If three zeros u<b<v existed, the midpoint m=(u+v)/2 would satisfy F(m)>0. Express b as a convex combination of m and the nearer endpoint u or v; its positive coefficient of F(m), together with the chord inequality, forces F(b)>0, a contradiction. Thus exactly the roots sqrt(2),beta occur. Their sum lies in (2+sqrt(2),4+sqrt(2)), a subset of [2,6), so D.

records.derivation: The frustum has radii3 and 6 and height3*sqrt(3), so its slant height is 6. Extend the cone: similar axial triangles give inner and outer developed radii6 and 12. Cone unfolding gives a sector of angle pi because the outer circular rim has circumference12*pi; diametrically opposite generators therefore differ by pi/2 in the developed angle. The straight developed chord enters the removed radius-6 disk and is inadmissible. Here is a global lower bound without assuming a new shortest-path theorem. Any continuous surface path lifts to the annular cone development with endpoint angular difference pi/2+k*pi for an integer k; after reflection its absolute angular difference is at least pi/2. It must cross the ray at angle pi/3 from A=(12,0). At a first such point P=(r/2,sqrt(3)*r/2), r>=6, the coordinate-distance formula gives AP^2=(r-6)^2+108>=108. Thus the path before P has length at least6*sqrt(3). The remaining path has net angular travel at least pi/6 and stays outside the radius-6 disk. Radial projection to that circle cannot increase length: for unit vectors u,v and r,s>=6, the squared distance identity |r*u-s*v|^2=(r-s)^2+r*s*|u-v|^2>=36*|u-v|^2 proves contraction for every chord. Apply it to every ordered path partition and take the supremum defining curve length; the projected path must cover circular angular travel at least pi/6, of length at least pi by the arc formula. Hence every path has length at least6*sqrt(3)+pi, including paths that wind or cross a development seam. Attainment is a tangent segment from A to the inner circle at angle pi/3, length 6*sqrt(3), followed by the inner-rim arc of angle pi/6, length pi. It stays within the annulus. Therefore the shortest length is 6*sqrt(3)+pi, E.

records.derivation: The target inequality is equivalent to 18<=x^2+y^2<=32, an annulus of area 14*pi. The board |x|+|y|<=8 is a square with vertices(8,0),(0,8),(-8,0),(0,-8), hence area 128 by four right triangles. To check containment algebraically, (|x|-|y|)^2>=0 implies(|x|+|y|)^2<=2*(x^2+y^2)<=64, so every target point lies in the board. Alternatively each boundary line of the board is at distance8/sqrt(2)=4*sqrt(2) from the origin, exactly the target outer radius; its disk is contained in all four bounding half-planes. Under the ordinary uniform-area dart convention, probability=14*pi/128=7*pi/64, so m+n=71, B. Boundaries have area zero.
